//: CLAIMS ABOUT THINGS THIS REPO DOES NOT CONTROL, and the version each was verified against.
A limitation written in prose ages exactly like a premise does, and nothing in this repo
noticed. The shape that fixes it came from showrunner (its INV20): a claim CANNOT be checked
automatically, but its SUBJECT can be versioned. Deciding whether 'rate_limits rides the
statusline payload' is still true needs a person. Deciding whether the release it was verified
against is the release running is four lines. That converts an unbounded duty -- stay vigilant
forever -- into a dated one: re-read these entries on the specific day the layer moves.
WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, since that sentence is itself the kind of claim it governs: it does not
check that any claim is TRUE, and it cannot. It removes the option of going stale QUIETLY.
`verified_against` is null on every entry below and that is not an oversight -- it is the
finding. These were read from the docs on 2026-07-29 and the version was never recorded, so
there is nothing to compare and the honest report says so. The first re-verification of any
entry fills it in and makes that entry checkable from then on. Do not back-fill it by guessing
which version was current that day; a stamp invented today is a number standing for nothing.
Each claim carries `ledger`: the exact LEDGER.md heading it accounts for. The suite
matches on THOSE, not on a count -- a count passes when one entry is added and
another removed, which is the shape of check that lies to you. A new VERIFIED or
RULED-OUT entry about the host therefore fails the run until somebody decides it.
A RUNG ABOVE VERSIONING, from showrunner: version the subject when you cannot reach it,
EXERCISE the subject when you can. A stamp records that the author verified something on the
author's machine and asserts it about a stranger's. An exercise checks it on the stranger's,
every run, and cannot go stale because there is no recorded answer to rot. Where a fact can be
provoked, the stamp is the weaker instrument -- so `exercised_by` outranks `verified_against`
on any claim that carries it, and the report says which one it is speaking from.
Only one of the six is exercisable today and the rest say so rather than implying otherwise:
the five RULED-OUT entries are absences, and an absence cannot be provoked -- observing that
no `claude usage` flag exists this run is not evidence it did not appear in the last release.
THE BOUND CORRECTED, by showrunner, after I told it 'exercise a presence, version an absence'.
That was generalised from a sample that agreed with itself. The discriminator is not presence
versus absence -- it is whether you CONTROL THE INPUT that would produce the effect. A
CONDITIONAL absence is exercisable: run the mechanism, show it fired, show the thing is still
not there. That pairing turns an absence into a DISCRIMINATION. An UNCONDITIONAL absence is not,
because the case where the fact is false is precisely the one you cannot construct.
So `exercisable` is three-valued and the middle one is a declared debt, not a pass: 'yes-not-yet'
means the control exists and nobody has written it. Saying four of these were unprovable was
wrong, and it was wrong in my own tool's output, which is the failure this file exists to name.
PER-CLAIM VERIFICATION, because the block stamp could not express a partial re-read. This file
promised that the first re-verification would fill in the null and make THAT entry checkable.
With one stamp for six claims, filling it in would have asserted six re-readings where one
happened — so the promise was unkeepable as written, which is a small instance of exactly what
this file exists to catch. Each claim now carries its own verified_on/verified_against, and the
block values remain the original reading for entries nobody has revisited.

claims.says: a fresh session costs ~38-40k input tokens before answering with NO MCP servers (39,556 at 2.1.319), and MCP and tool definitions add on top of that in proportion to what is configured: ~41k more with 32 servers and 373 tools
claims.breaks: the recommendation against spawning sessions to sample usage rests on this floor; if it dropped to near zero the objection would weaken and a polling probe might be fine
claims.ledger: A fresh Claude Code session costs ~31.5k INPUT tokens before it answers anything, and ~24k of that is irreducible
claims.verified_how: CONTROLLED RE-READ at 2.1.319, after game_loop#146 reported 81,032 input-side and called the floor refuted. That run had 32 MCP servers and 373 tools in init, so it could not separate the host from the configuration. The control, run by me on the same 2.1.319 binary: `claude -p 'reply with the single word: ok' --output-format json --strict-mcp-config --settings '{"disableAllHooks":true}'` gave 39,556 (2 in / 15,414 cache-create / 24,140 cache-read). So the HOST floor holds at about the 2.1.251 figure (37,105), and the reported 81k is ~41k of MCP and tool definitions. What is REFUTED is the old decomposition's 'MCP schemas are ~1.2k': that was true of a light configuration, and it scales with what a machine has configured. One run each, so treat the split as loose. The recommendation stands and is stronger on a heavily configured machine. TWO METHOD NOTES. With hooks disabled the run took about 1-6 s, so the old 'longer than ten minutes, run unbounded' note was hook time, not the model call. And here --output-format json returned ONE OBJECT whose usage is at the top level, while the reporter saw an array of events (an init event, rate_limit_event, assistant, result); something in their settings changes the shape, so read usage from the result element when it is a list.
claims.exercisable_why: CONDITIONAL and exercisable, and the CHEAP path is now known. Previously recorded as not-yet because the exercise spends the resource it measures and needs network and credentials. That reasoning was sound and INCOMPLETE: the statusline payload's context_window carries ABSOLUTE counts (total_input_tokens, context_window_size, current_usage.input_tokens), not only used_percentage — read out of 2.1.223's own embedded schema on 2026-08-13. So `limitprobe` already spawns a FRESH session and its render already carries this claim's number: the exercise can ride a spawn that is being paid for anyway, instead of buying one. Still a debt, but a debt with a costed route rather than a reason to leave it alone.
claims.exercised_by: `claude -p 'reply with the single word: ok' --output-format json --strict-mcp-config --settings '{"disableAllHooks":true}'` on the binary at CLAUDE_CODE_EXECPATH, summing input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + cache_read_input_tokens from the result (the top-level object, or the element with type 'result' when the output is an array). Repeat without --strict-mcp-config for the configuration's MCP and tool share.

previous_reading.verified_how: EXERCISED at 2.1.251, two probes as documented, and the result is PARTIAL with one half REFUTED as measurable. THE TOTAL HOLDS: baseline 37,105 input-side (2 in / 17,109 cache-create / 19,994 cache-read) against 38,371 recorded at 2.1.246 — a fresh session still costs ~37-38k before answering, which is what the headline asserts. THE MCP SHARE COULD NOT BE MEASURED, and the attempt says why: --strict-mcp-config came back at 38,559, HIGHER than the baseline, so the difference is -1,454. MCP schemas cannot subtract tokens. The two runs' cache-create/cache-read split differs by ~3k (17,109/19,994 versus 15,585/22,972), so run-to-run variance in cache warmth is larger than the ~1.2k share the exercise subtracts for. One pair of probes cannot isolate it; the earlier ~1.2k figure came from one pair too, and this result is the reason to doubt the method rather than the earlier number. THE DECOMPOSITION IS THE PART THAT MOVED: 'of which ~24.9k is irreducible base preamble read from cache' reads ~20.0k here, and given the variance above, that field should be treated as unstable rather than as a measured constant. Also worth the next reader's time: each probe takes longer than ten minutes, so it must be run unbounded — a 10-minute timeout kills it and leaves an empty file that reads exactly like a failure. Two of my four attempts today died that way.

claims.says: the statusline payload's context_window carries ABSOLUTE token counts — total_input_tokens, total_output_tokens, context_window_size, and current_usage {input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens} — alongside used_percentage/remaining_percentage
claims.source: read in the running binary at 2.1.223 (the client's own embedded payload schema)
claims.breaks: the harness reads only used_percentage, so every absolute token question is currently answered by inference or by spawning something. If these fields moved, any future usage work resting on them silently loses its measurement
claims.ledger: The statusline payload exposes only a PERCENTAGE of context used
claims.exercisable_why: EXERCISED 2026-08-24. Our own limit probe records the raw block to probe/context-window.json, uninterpreted, so a later reading is a real observation rather than a memory of one — which is exactly what closed it.
claims.verified_how: Reported by the drops owner agent in game_loop#146, who read it on a machine whose session was served by the 2.1.319 binary (attributed by PID with lsof). probe/context-window.json observed 2026-11-09 15:48 with host_version 2.1.319 carries total_input_tokens, total_output_tokens, context_window_size and all four current_usage fields. This one NAMES its build, which the 2.1.251 capture could not.

saggar.subject: saggar (the terminal manager `successor` can hand a session to)
saggar.verified_against: `saggar --help` at ~/.local/bin/saggar (2026-08-27), four live agent terminals on 2026-08-26, and ~/.saggar/claude-presence-hook.sh (rewritten 2026-08-26 11:25)
saggar.why_it_matters: `successor`'s saggar-agent mode is the handover a human is meant to find later, and what that terminal is CALLED is the whole of finding it. saggar shipped `agent --title` on 2026-08-26 and this repo spent a day documenting the gap instead of closing it — every handover opened a terminal named "Terminal". If the flag moves again, the handovers go unfindable and the only thing that would notice is a person scanning a row of identical terminals.

claims.says: BROKEN 2026-08-26 by a saggar update, on exactly the condition this entry named for itself, and CLOSED 2026-08-27 by the code catching up. `saggar agent` takes `--title <title>` and it DOES name the displayed terminal: two live agent terminals opened with a --title read back from `saggar list --json` under those exact strings, while two UNTITLED probes launched the same hour stayed at saggar's default "Terminal" throughout. For a day after that measurement the repo carried the correct EXPLANATION and the wrong CALL — `successor` printed "NOT SET FROM HERE, that is OUR gap" while `_saggar_agent` invoked the untitled form, so every handover opened a terminal called "Terminal". Found by the human, not by this checkout, because the test asserted stdout and the gap was in argv. `_saggar_agent` now passes `--title <title> -- <task>`, and test/run.py's fake saggar records "$@" so the assertion is on the argument list rather than on the paragraph describing it.
claims.source: `saggar --help` at ~/.local/bin/saggar (agent --title, and `--` ends agent options before the task), read 2026-08-27; plus four live agent terminals read back from `saggar list --json` on 2026-08-26
claims.breaks: What would break the CURRENT reading: if --title stopped overriding, or were overwritten once Claude titles the conversation, or if the `--` separator were dropped from the CLI. Untested: whether the title survives a saggar restart or a `--session-id` terminal reuse. Also unproven in the override direction — a conversation title is not stored on disk anywhere readable (~/.claude/history.jsonl holds prompts, not titles), so it could not be confirmed that the 42-turn probe ever generated one for --title to beat. What is measured is that the explicit name held where the default did not, and that the flag is on the wire.
claims.ledger: Anything game_loop passes to `saggar agent` names the saggar terminal
claims.exercisable_why: EXERCISED 2026-08-25 by the act the earlier entry said would be needed: a live handover through the running app, with the terminal's name read back from `saggar list --json`. It costs a real claude session, so it is a thing a person re-runs, never a gate
claims.exercised_by: `saggar agent claude --title "<name>" -- <task>`, then `saggar list --json` for the terminal's name
claims.verified_against: `saggar --help` at ~/.local/bin/saggar on 2026-08-27; four live agent terminals on 2026-08-26; the installed presence hook at ~/.saggar/claude-presence-hook.sh (rewritten 2026-08-26 11:25)
claims.verified_how: RE-READ 2026-08-27 off the CLI on this machine's PATH, which the 2026-08-26 reading could not reach: `saggar agent <agent> <task…>` with `--title <title>` and `--` documented as ending agent options before the task. The live four-terminal exercise behind the naming behaviour is the 2026-08-26 one and was NOT re-run here — what 2026-08-27 adds is the flag's presence and the fact that game_loop now sends it.
claims.exercise_note: the falsifying case is constructible and was constructed: a prompt whose subject is distinctive. If a name ever came from the caller, the same handover with --title set would show it
claims.superseded_note: The 2026-08-25 finding that Claude's own conversation title names the terminal is NOT confirmed live any more either: ~/.saggar/chat-info/ has not been written since 2026-08-24, so the status-line bridge that carried it is no longer the path saggar uses. Long-lived sessions still show conversation titles in `saggar list`, so some path still exists; which one was not traced.
